newsitem.title: USA: Maine won't freeze minimum wage at restaurants - Gov.
newsitem.headline: Maine won't freeze minimum wage at restaurants - Gov.

text.p: Gov. Angus King Tuesday refused to sign legislation that would have prevented many Maine restaurant workers from benefiting from the pending increase in the minimum wage.
King said that after two weeks of difficult deliberations he decided he could not sign the measure that would freeze the minimum wage of waiters and waitresses who rely on tips at $2.13 an hour.

Maine law allows restaurants to pay tipped workers less than the federal minimum wage, but requires the lower "tipping wage" be increased when the federal level goes up. The wage is scheduled to increase $.25 in October and $.20 in October 1997.
Restaurant owners had complained the increase would harm Maine's valuable tourism industry. The measure's opponents said Maine workers deserved to get the same increase as other U.S. workers.

King said he was concerned workers had not been warned lawmakers would vote on the wage freeze when they met in a Sept 5 special session that was supposed to review the state's forest management rules.
The governor told reporters there were "compelling arguments" on both sides of the debate, and he might reconsider his position if similar legislation was proposed next year.
